name: The Liquidity Trap
statement: When interest rates hit zero, printing more money just gets hoarded and monetary policy stops working.
statementAccent: printing more money just gets hoarded and monetary policy stops working
meaning: A liquidity trap is a situation in monetary economics, described by John Maynard Keynes, in which nominal interest rates are at or near zero, so conventional monetary policy, expanding the money supply to lower rates, becomes ineffective at stimulating the economy. Because rates cannot fall meaningfully further, people and banks prefer to hold cash rather than bonds or investments, so additional money injected into the economy is simply hoarded rather than spent or lent. The metaphor is that monetary policy is pushing on a string. Keynes set out the concept in his 1936 General Theory, and John Hicks formalised it in his 1937 IS-LM model as the flat portion of the LM curve, where monetary expansion has no effect on rates or output. Japan since the 1990s and much of the developed world after the 2008 financial crisis are commonly cited as real-world liquidity traps.
mechanism: At very low or near-zero interest rates, the demand for money becomes highly, even perfectly, elastic: people are willing to hold any additional quantity of money rather than bonds. This is because bonds yield almost nothing and carry the risk of capital loss if rates rise, since bond prices fall when rates rise, so cash and short-term bonds become near-perfect substitutes. Consequently, when the central bank injects more money, there is no incentive to lend or spend it, rates do not fall further, and the usual transmission from money to interest rates to investment and consumption breaks down. In the IS-LM framework this is the horizontal segment of the LM curve, along which shifting the money supply leaves the equilibrium interest rate and output unchanged. Because conventional monetary policy is impotent, economists argue that fiscal policy, government borrowing and spending, becomes the more effective tool, and central banks turn to unconventional measures such as quantitative easing, forward guidance, and negative interest rates to try to escape the trap.

examples.text: With rates near zero and bonds yielding almost nothing but risking loss if rates rise, people hoard cash, so new money does not get spent or lent.
Japan's near-zero-rate stagnation since the 1990s is the canonical modern liquidity trap, with conventional monetary policy struggling to revive demand.
Following the 2008 crisis, near-zero rates across the developed world led economists to argue much of it was in a liquidity trap, prompting quantitative easing.

variants.name: The zero lower bound
variants.text: The modern framing in terms of nominal interest rates constrained near zero, where conventional rate cuts are exhausted and unconventional tools are needed.

variants.name: The IS-LM flat LM curve
variants.text: Hicks's formalisation, in which the liquidity trap is the horizontal segment of the LM curve where monetary expansion does not change rates or output.

whyItMatters: The liquidity trap is a central concept in Keynesian macroeconomics and in the analysis of monetary policy at the zero lower bound, explaining why central banks can lose their usual power to fight recessions. When rates are already near zero, cutting them further is impossible and pumping in more money is hoarded, so the standard levers fail, which is why deep downturns like Japan's lost decades and the aftermath of 2008 posed such difficult policy problems. The concept underpins the case for fiscal policy as the more effective response in such conditions and motivated the unconventional tools, quantitative easing, forward guidance, and negative rates, that central banks deployed to try to escape the trap. It also frames a long-running debate: monetarists like Milton Friedman dispute how binding the trap really is, arguing monetary policy can still work through other channels, making the liquidity trap a focal point in disputes over how to combat recessions.

working.text: let nominal interest rates fall to or near zero, exhausting the room for conventional rate cuts.
note that with bonds yielding nothing and risking loss, people hold any extra money as cash rather than spending or lending it.
recognise that conventional monetary policy is impotent, so fiscal policy and unconventional measures like quantitative easing are used to respond.

limits: Whether liquidity traps are real and important is debated. Monetarists, notably Milton Friedman, argue that monetary policy retains power even at zero short-term rates, since the central bank can expand the monetary base and operate on longer-term or riskier assets, so any nonzero rate along the yield curve provides a channel. The efficacy of unconventional tools like quantitative easing is itself contested, and the trap's practical bite depends on expectations, the state of the banking system, and fiscal capacity. The concept is often analysed within the stylised IS-LM model, which abstracts from many complications. So the liquidity trap is a widely used and influential framework for thinking about policy at the zero lower bound, but its existence, severity, and the best escape routes remain matters of active dispute.
misreadings: A liquidity trap does not mean all policy is powerless; it means conventional interest-rate cuts fail, while fiscal policy and unconventional measures may still act. It is not simply that rates are low, but that they are so low that extra money is hoarded rather than transmitted to spending. And it is contested: monetarists argue monetary policy still works through other channels, so treating the liquidity trap as a proven, absolute wall, or as a reason nothing can be done, misstates a concept whose importance and remedies are debated.
origin: Described by John Maynard Keynes in his 1936 General Theory and formalised by John Hicks in his 1937 IS-LM model as the flat LM curve; invoked for Japan's stagnation since the 1990s and the aftermath of the 2008 crisis.
